title: Catching up with AI
text:
Why this site exists
For the last 15 years I have worked in bioinformatics and biomedical data science, building data analysis pipelines and supporting scientific research. During that time, artificial intelligence evolved rapidly — especially in areas like deep learning and, more recently, generative AI.
Like many scientists working with data, I realized at some point that I had developed a knowledge gap. I was comfortable with statistical modeling, genomics data analysis, and scientific computing — but the whole ecosystem around large language models (LLMs) and AI-assisted workflows had largely evolved outside my day-to-day work.
This notebook is my way of catching up. It collects my notes along the way — part learning log, part technical guide. I try to document not just what I learn, but also how I do it, what I find confusing, and what actually turns out to be useful in practice.
Here is the rough path I followed:

title: Catching up with AI
text:
A short history of generative AI – I started by simply using using tools ChatGPT [link] and Perplexity [link] to get some background: how we got here, which milestones really mattered, and who the main players and models are today.
ChatGPT, the basics – I subscribed to ChatGPT Pro (22 EUR/month) and worked through the beginner tutorials at the OpenAI Academy [link] (free). This was quick but surprisingly solid to build a foundation and understand what the tool can do (and what not) and how to use the interface.
Prompt engineering – To learn what I call “The art of talking to the machine”, I subscribed to Coursera [link] (42 EUR/month) and took some basic and advanced courses on prompt engineering by Jules White, including how to create custom AI assistants (Custom GPTs) and build trustworthy genAI. This is where I started to get some real insights
Data analysis workflows with ChatGPT – Also by Jules White, these courses go deeper into practical workflows, showing how to use ChatGPT (via Code Interpreter) together with external tools for real data analysis tasks (and real magic).
Reflections - A complication of insights and resources on how to provide appropriate rail guards for generative AI, AI agents and agentic AI and how (in my opinion) generative AI should be used ethically

title: 2  Prompt Engineering
text:
2.1 How LLMs Work (Conceptual + Technical Basics)
Based on my notes from the coursera courses ’Prompt Engineering with ChatGTP’, ‘Advanced Prompt Engineering’, and ‘Build Your CustomGPT’ by Jules White(Vanderbuilt University). Adapted with ChatGTP.
Example:
If you write “The mitochondria is the …”, the model predicts “powerhouse of the cell” because this phrase has a high probability in the training data.

title: 2  Prompt Engineering
text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text by predicting the next token based on patterns learned from training data.
→ They operate autoregressively: each generated token is appended to the context and used to predict the next one.
ChatGPT = Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer:

Self-attention computes weighted relationships across all tokens, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the context.
Positional encodings inject information about token order, enabling the model to represent sequences rather than bags of words.

Internal processing pipeline:

Text → tokenization → numerical embeddings → stacked transformer layers → probability distribution over the next token.

Probability, not understanding:

The model does not “know” facts; it estimates which continuation is most likely given the context and its training distribution.

Training objective:

Minimize cross-entropy loss, pushing predicted token probabilities closer to the tokens observed in large-scale text corpora.

Determinism vs. randomness:

Sampling parameters (e.g. temperature, top-k/top-p) influence how deterministic or creative the output appears.

title: 2  Prompt Engineering
text:
2.2 Prompt Engineering (Purpose and Practice)

“The art of talking to the machine.”

Prompt engineering aims to:

Produce reliable, repeatable, and useful outputs despite inherent nondeterminism.
Increase predictability, consistency, and task alignment.
Clearly encode task intent, context, constraints, and output structure.
Reduce ambiguity and lower the risk of hallucinations.

Example 1 (general):
Instead of:
> “Explain CRISPR.”
Better:
> “Act as a molecular biologist. Explain CRISPR to a motivated high-school student in 3 bullet points.”
Example 2 (technical):
Instead of:
> “Explain PCA.”
Better:
> “Provide a mathematically grounded explanation of PCA for an R programmer. Include eigenvectors, variance decomposition, and a 3-line R code example.”

title: 3  Prompt Pattern (practical)
text: 3.1 Core Prompt Patterns

title: 3  Prompt Pattern (practical)
text:
3.1.1 Persona Pattern
Helps control tone, expertise, cultural assumptions.
Example:
“Act as a senior bioinformatician experienced in single-cell epigenomics. Provide actionable suggestions.”


3.1.2 Audience Persona Pattern
Tell GPT who you are so explanations match your background.
Example:
“Assume I am new to machine learning but familiar with R and statistics. Explain what a transformer is.”


3.1.3 Question Refinement
GPT improves your question. Useful for technical tasks where question quality matters.
Example:
“When I ask you something unclear, suggest a sharper version first and ask if I want to use it.”


3.1.4 Few-shot Prompting
You show examples (introduce training data) → GPT follows your pattern. Useful for labeling, transformations, extraction tasks.
Example:
Input: ATGCGT
Output: reversed sequence: TGCGTA

Prompt:
Input: AACCAT
Output:
GPT continues with the intended pattern.


3.1.5 Flipped Interaction
GPT asks you the questions.
Example:
“Ask me clarifying questions until you can design a workshop outline. When you have enough information, present the final outline.”


3.1.6 Chain of Thought
Explicit reasoning steps.
Example:
“Show your reasoning in short bullet points and end with a boxed final answer.”
Helps when solving problems or planning.


3.1.7 ReAct Prompting
Reason → take external action → reason → answer.
Example:
“Search PubMed for recent papers on DNA methylation in HSCs, summarize top 3 findings, and explain how they relate to AML biology.”
(Assuming GPT has tools activated.)


3.1.8 Alternative Approaches
Ask for multiple solutions. (or strategy for approaches)
Example:
“Propose 5 different ways to create a metadata-capture workflow for a small lab, ranked by feasibility.”
Great for brainstorming and problem solving.


3.1.9 Evaluation Pattern
Use examples or rubrics to grade model output.
Example:
“Here are 3 example abstracts. Score the following abstract for clarity (1–5), structure (1–5), scientific accuracy (1–5). Provide justification.”


3.1.10 Game-play Pattern
Turn tasks into structured exercises. Define rules.
Example:
“We are going to play a game:
I describe a lab workflow, you generate 5 mistakes a junior researcher might make, and how to fix them.”


3.1.11 Recipe Pattern
Stepwise instructions with gaps.
Example:
“Fill in missing steps for this workflow:


Load FASTQ files

Align using BWA

Generate BAM summary”




3.1.12 Template Pattern
Use placeholders → consistent output.
Example:
Mutation Summary
Gene: <GENE>
Variant: <VARIANT>
Impact: <IMPACT>
Evidence: <QUOTES FROM ARTICLE>

title: 3  Prompt Pattern (practical)
text:
3.2 Text Manipulation Patterns

3.2.1 Semantic Filter
Remove or replace specific elements.
Example:
“Remove all dates from the text but change as little as possible.”


3.2.2 Meta-language Pattern
Define a micro-language the LLM should learn.
Example:
“When I write ‘QC-S1’, interpret it as: run initial QC on sequencing files and summarize FastQC results.”

title: 3  Prompt Pattern (practical)
text:
3.3 Verifier Pattern

3.3.1 Cognitive Verifier Pattern
Meta-reasoning pattern where the model is instructed to generate an answer, independently verify, critique, or test that answer and revise if needed. Focuses on error detection, not explanation.
Typical prompt form:
“First provide an answer. Then verify it by checking assumptions, edge cases, and alternative interpretations.” “Critically review your own solution and correct any mistakes.”
What it does well - Reduces hallucinations - Improves factual and logical reliability - Surfaces hidden assumptions - Excellent for high-stakes outputs
What it is not - Not primarily about explaining reasoning to the user - Verification may be concise or structured rather than narrative
Example:
Answer: X
Verification: - Check assumptions → valid - Alternative method → same result - Edge cases → none violated
Conclusion: Answer stands.


3.3.2 Fact Checking Pattern
Force verification.
Steps:

Extract facts
Compare with source
Flag inconsistencies
Insert verified fact list at the end

Example:
“Extract all factual statements from the text and list any that need verification.”

title: 3  Prompt Pattern (practical)
text:
3.4 Workflows

3.4.1 Working on smaller pieces
Outline Expansion Start small, expand in pieces.
Example:
“Here is the outline for a workshop. Expand only section 2. Keep the rest unchanged.”


3.4.2 Tail Generation
Add automatic “post-processing.”
Example:
“When done summarizing, also produce a 3-item action list.”

title: 4  Prompt Pattern (technical)
text:
4.1 Core Prompt Pattern
A compact, engineering-oriented overview

title: 4  Prompt Pattern (technical)
text:
4.1.1 Persona Pattern (Functional Control)
Define computational role + constraints.
Example:
“Act as a senior data engineer. Output only SQL, no explanations.”


4.1.2 Audience Persona Pattern (Adjust Explanation Level)
Tells the model who the target reader is.
Example:
“Explain transformer attention to someone familiar with matrix multiplication but new to NLP.”


4.1.3 Flipped Interaction Pattern (Information Acquisition)
Useful when task requires parameters or architecture definition.
Example:
“Ask me all required questions to define a Snakemake workflow. Then generate the final workflow.”


4.1.4 Question Refinement Pattern (Error Reduction)
GPT rewrites your question to reduce ambiguity.
Example:
“Before answering, propose a more precise version of my question optimized for computational reproducibility.”


4.1.5 Cognitive Verifier Pattern (Structured Reasoning)
Model decomposes problem → produces final synthesized answer.
Useful to check the model’s reasoning. Improves the output.
Example:
“Break the question into technical sub-questions (≤5), answer them, then produce the final integrated explanation.”


4.1.6 Few-Shot Pattern (Pattern Imitation)
Provide input/output examples → model induces rule.
Example:
Input: “ATGGCT”
Output: reverse_complement: “AGCCAT”

Input: “CGTAAT”
Output:
GPT generalizes rule across new inputs.


4.1.7 Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Pattern (Explain Reasoning)
Model outputs intermediate reasoning (optional).
Example:
“Show your reasoning in short bullet points and end with a boxed final answer.”


4.1.8 ReAct Pattern (Reason + Tool Use)
LLM reasons → takes actions (search, code execution) → final answer.
Example:
“Search the latest ENCODE metadata for a DNase-seq dataset, summarize QC metrics, then evaluate quality.”


4.1.9 Evaluation Pattern (Auto-Grading Models)
Provide criteria or examples → GPT scores candidates.
Example:
“Evaluate the following three pipeline descriptions for clarity (1–5), modularity (1–5), reproducibility (1–5). Justify each score.”


4.1.10 Template Pattern (Deterministic Structure)
Force GPT to output in a machine-readable or human-readable schema.
Example:
{
“task”: “<TASK>”,
“inputs”: \["\<INPUT_1\>", "\<INPUT_2\>"\],
“steps”: \["\<STEP_1\>", "\<STEP_2\>"\],
“expected_output”: “<OUTPUT>”
}


4.1.11 Meta-Language Pattern (Define Custom Syntax)
You define a symbolic shorthand → model learns mapping.
Example:
“Interpret ‘QC-S1’ as: run FastQC → summarize per-base content → output 3 metrics.”


4.1.12 Recipe Pattern (Pipeline Definition)
Fill missing steps in a workflow.
Example:
“Insert the two missing steps in this pipeline:

Load FASTQ
Align with BWA
Generate BAM summary”



4.1.13 Alternative Approaches Pattern (Algorithmic Exploration)
Generate multiple candidate solutions.
Example:
“Provide 4 alternative strategies for building a FAIR-compliant metadata capture workflow. Rank by implementation cost.”

title: 4  Prompt Pattern (technical)
text:
4.2 Text & Data Manipulation Patterns

4.2.1 Semantic Filter
Remove or transform only the targeted elements.
Example:
“Remove all patient identifiers but keep clinical meaning intact.”


4.2.2 Tail Pattern (Post-Processing)
Append additional required content automatically.
Example:
“After summarizing the paper, append a list of unresolved questions.”


4.2.3 Fact-Checking Pattern
Extract facts → verify → append fact list.
Example:
“Extract all factual claims from the text and mark those that require verification due to missing sources.”

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.1 Intro
User-configured versions of ChatGPT that behave like a specialized assistant for a specific task, domain, or workflow—without writing code. Persistent behaviour.
Can be created through the ChatGTP app.
/
Components:
Use cases:

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
Aspect
ChatGPT
Custom GPT




Purpose
General-purpose assistant
Task- or domain-specific assistant


Instructions
Provided ad hoc per chat
Persistent, predefined instructions


Knowledge
Generic model knowledge
Optional uploaded documents & references


Consistency
Varies between chats
Stable, repeatable behavior


Prompting effort
Repeated each session
One-time setup


Tool access
User-controlled per chat
Preconfigured tools


Hallucination risk
Higher (open-ended)
Lower (scoped + constrained)


Best use case
Exploration, quick questions
Workflows, training, institutional use






Personality: tone + style
Prompt template: instructions, constraints
Data sources: files, knowledge bases
Actions: external tools



Automating bioinformatics reports
Turning handwritten notes into Google Docs
Cleaning up metadata

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.2 Personality
Customize how your chatbot interacts:

Confidence: a) assured, b) measured
Amicability: a)friendly, b) neutral
Professionalism: a) formal, b) casual
Interactivity: a) engaging, b) informative
Transparency: a) adaptive, b) consistent
Lexicography: a) specialized, b) universal

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.3 Structuring Input & Output

5.3.1 Input Pattern
Prompt instructs GPT to ask for missing info.
Example:
“Before writing, ask me for the dataset description.”


5.3.2 Structured Output (tables, checklists, format)**
Makes results more usable.
Example (table):
| Step | Description | Tools |
|——|————-|——-|
| 1 | QC | FastQC |
| 2 | Alignment | BWA |
Use markdown formatting options (headers, tables, links, footnotes)!
This is useful when prompting for reusable, clean, publication-ready output.

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.4 Tabular data analysis
LLMs can understand tables if provided clearly.
Example:
“Using the table below, predict the missing column ‘Cell type’.”
They can also create synthetic datasets to help test pipelines.

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.5 In-Context Learning with Tabular Data
Provide columns + examples → model deduces hidden rules.
Example:
“Given columns A and B, predict column C (protein class) based on observed patterns.”

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.6 Synthetic Data Generation
Bootstrap ML experiments or testing.
Example:
“Generate a synthetic metadata table of 50 samples with fields: donor_age, diagnosis, cell_type, library_size.”

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.7 ML with Prompts (Your Course Notes)
Classification via Prompting

Good for simple yes/no or category labeling.

Example:
“Label each comment as ‘informative’, ‘spam’, or ‘uncertain’.”
Clustering via Prompting

Model groups items into meaningful clusters.

Example:
“Cluster the following 30 job descriptions into 5 roles and output an ASCII taxonomy tree.”
Prediction via Prompting

Model extrapolates patterns.

Example:
“Given the engagement metrics for existing workshop titles, propose 3 new course titles likely to perform well.”

title: 5  CustomGPTs
text:
5.8 Benchmarking GPT (Your “Test the GPT” Notes)
Things to test:

Factual accuracy
Reasoning
Creativity
Cultural/linguistic alignment
Output structure
Handling of adversarial or ambiguous input

Example:
“Test whether the model stays consistent when given conflicting instructions.”
Built your own testerGPT to benchmark other customGPTs!

5.8.1 Reliability & Safety
Preventing hallucinations

Provide all key information first.
Ask user to confirm before acting.

Escape Valves to avoid forced answers.
Example:
“If missing, respond with <N/A>.”
Boundaries

For safety, compliance, correctness.
Useful in regulated areas (e.g., healthcare, legal, institutional guidelines).

Example:
“Do not provide clinical guidance. If asked, offer general information and suggest contacting a medical professional.”
Ambiguity Handling

Identify it
Ask for clarification or fall back on <N/A>



5.8.2 Conflict Resolution
When documents/ inputs conflict:

Use newest
If one contains the needed topic and the other not, use the relevant one
State uncertainty explicitly



5.8.3 Adversarial Input Prevention

Add railguards
Disable functionality beyond scope
Avoid being tricked into harmful or nonsensical replies

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
text:
6.1 General Principles of Working with generative AI
My notes from the Coursera courses Advanced Data Analysis with ChatGPT and Building Trustworthy AI (Code Interpreter) by Jules White. Digitized from handwritten material via mobile photos and organized into a coherent structure using ChatGPT (customGPT: “Notes Organizer”).
Synopsis: How to use ChatGPT effectively for data analysis, document processing, workflow planning, and creative problem-solving, and outline key principles, tools, and frameworks (such as ACHIEVE and ETAC) that help AI augment human reasoning while maintaining accuracy and control.
Fundamentals
Treat Code Interpreter as an internal assistant
Think of the Code Interpreter as a smart intern that needs clear instructions:

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
text:
“LLMs do not generate answers, LLMs generate text. Some of the text might provide useful answers”(Jules White)
LLM output has an inherent random component (LLMs predict, and the same prompt may not provide the exact same output)
Using generative AI implys taking ownership of the output.




Break tasks down step-by-step.
Provide all necessary context and information upfront – data files, constraints, goals, examples.
Ask for detailed feedback, e.g. “What could be improved about this figure?”
Don’t expect perfection. Plan to iterate with it.
Always review results for accuracy, plausibility, and errors.
Be explicit about:

What you want to achieve.
How you want results presented (tables, plots, summaries, slides).
Any constraints (runtime, file formats, colour schemes, etc.).

Provide escape valves

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
section: 6.2 Working with Data Files, Documents, Media and Zip Files
text:
6.2 Working with Data Files, Documents, Media and Zip Files

6.2.1 Working with Data Files and Visualizations

6.2.1.1 Uploading and exploring data
Typical workflow with Code Interpreter:

Upload a dataset (csv) and ask:

“Read this file and explain the structure of the data.”
“Show me the columns, data types, and basic statistics.”

Ask for interesting visualizations:

“Create several interesting plots that could be useful for exploratory analysis.”
“Try a histogram, a boxplot, and a scatterplot matrix.”


You can then iterate:

“Refine the labels and axes.”
“Use a harmonized colour scheme.”
“Order categories in a meaningful way.”



6.2.1.2 Adding narrative text and presentations
You can ask ChatGPT to help with presentation-ready outputs:

“Insert each visualization into a slide and write a short caption explaining what it shows.”
“Update my existing slides with a short narrative for each plot.”
“Use consistent terminology and colour coding across all slides.”

Example prompt:

“Create a one-slide summary for each of these plots, explaining what the viewer should take away. Use clear language suitable for a multidisciplinary biomedical audience.”




6.2.2 Working with Documents

6.2.2.1 Documents as objects vs. documents as knowledge
Two levels of interaction with documents:

Document as an object

Operations: rename, move, download, edit, zip/unzip.

Document as knowledge

Operations: analyze, summarize, outline, extract key statements, compare sections, etc.


Being aware of this distinction helps you design useful prompts.


6.2.2.2 Useful document prompts
Examples:

“Extract this PDF to plain text and tell me what it contains at a high level.”
“Reread the text and break it down into the smallest meaningful sections with headings.”
“Create an outline of the document.”
“Identify contradictions, gaps, or redundancies.”
“Highlight all places where inclusion criteria are mentioned and summarise them.”

This improves:

Reasoning – you understand the structure more clearly.
Verification – easier to check that all key information is captured.
Navigation – easier to find where specific concepts live.




6.2.3 Using Canvas in ChatGPT
Canvas is useful for interactive editing and document development.

6.2.3.1 Basic Canvas workflow

Open Canvas.
Paste or import your text (or upload a document to extract text).
Enter a prompt to modify the text or to ask for comments/suggestions.
Edit the text manually or accept/reject suggested changes.
Optionally upload additional documents for context (e.g. guidelines, previous drafts).
Enter more prompts to adjust tone, clarity, length, or structure.
Use the Canvas controls (e.g. icons in the lower corner) to adjust text length and polish.



6.2.3.2 Two main Canvas entry paths

Upload a document + prompt
> “Extract the text from this document into Canvas and clean up formatting.”
Copy & paste text directly
Then iterate with prompts to refine.




6.2.4 Structured Data Workflows

6.2.4.1 Understanding tables
Useful prompts:

“Read and explain the structure of this table.”
“Describe each column, including data type and potential problems.”
“Identify missing values, inconsistent labels, and outliers.”

Then:

“Calculate derived variables step-by-step and show intermediate tables.”
“Visualise the relationship between variable X and Y, including confidence intervals.”



6.2.4.2 Example workflow

Load dataset (CSV, TSV, Excel, etc.).
Ask for an overview (dimensions, column types, missingness).
Clean: standardise categories, handle missing values.
Derive new variables (ratios, differences, grouping codes).
Visualise key relationships.
Summarise results in natural language.




6.2.5 Working with Media and Zip Archives

6.2.5.1 Video workflows
Typical operations:

“Extract N frames from this video, evenly spaced.”
“Display the extracted frames.”
“Resize each image to 300 px wide while preserving aspect ratio.”
“Convert to grayscale and increase contrast by 30%.”

This is useful for:

Creating thumbnails.
Quick quality checks.
Preparing training data for image models.



6.2.5.2 Zip archives
Zip archives are handy for batch operations:

Zip multiple outputs into a single file for download.
Ask ChatGPT to propose a folder structure and better filenames.

Example prompt:

“Resize all images to 300 px width, rename them systematically, and put them into a zip file for download. Suggest a clear naming scheme based on sample ID and time point.”

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
text: 6.3 Workflows and Planning

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
section: 6.4 Check: Bringing Information into the Conversation
text:
6.4 Check: Bringing Information into the Conversation
Useful operations:

“Read this long text.”
“Summarize it in X bullet points.”
“Present the key information back to me in a way that I can quickly verify.”
“Create an index of where specific information (e.g. inclusion criteria, endpoints) can be found.”

This helps to:

Improve reasoning.
Support verification and auditing.
Create better documentation and overviews.


6.4.1 The ETAC Framework for workflows Human + AI Process Planning
Think of the overall human–AI workflow as:
E – Extract → T – Transform → A – AI / Analyze → C – Create

6.4.1.1 Extract: modalities and operations

Documents (docx, pdf, txt)

Text extraction
Metadata extraction
Entity recognition

Video (mp4, avi)

Frame extraction
Object detection
(Sometimes) face recognition

Audio (mp3, wav)

Speech-to-text
Noise reduction
Feature extraction

Datasets (csv, tsv, json, xlsx)

Load data
Preprocess
Feature engineering

Images (jpg, png, etc.)

Object detection
Segmentation
Feature extraction




6.4.1.2 Transform: data and images

Structured data

Clean and normalise
Drop or merge columns
Recode values
Compute derived features

Images

Subselect regions (ROI)
Crop and resize
Adjust contrast, brightness, etc.


Always prefer small, controlled steps that you can undo or repeat.



6.4.2 Analyze: From raw material to insight
Analysis-related operations include:

Find ambiguities and inconsistencies.
Analyse and summarise content.
Raise clarifying questions for the user.
Generate examples and counter-examples.

You can also maintain a “library” or mental catalogue of:

File types
Common operations
Good default workflows



6.4.3 Planning Workflows – Human and AI Roles

6.4.3.1 Human planning

Lay out the process manually first:

Inputs
Intermediate artefacts
Outputs

Decide what you want to control vs. what AI can suggest.



6.4.3.2 AI planning
Ask ChatGPT:

“Propose a detailed step-by-step plan for this task.”

Then refine:

Expand each bullet into 2–3 actionable substeps.
Ensure each step is something:

You can perform, or
The Python environment can perform.

Turn the result into an actionable plan or checklist.
Verify that the sequence of step is executable




6.4.4 AI Planning Techniques and Iteration
Good practice when executing a plan with Code Interpreter:

Execute steps one by one.
Save results of each step into separate files (for reproducibility and debugging).
At the beginning of each step:

Reflect on prior output.
Check alignment with goals.

If something breaks:

Stop, diagnose, fix the step.
Then continue.


You can also:

Store the plan itself in a separate file for later reuse.
Use “flipped interaction”: ask AI to improve your plan, rather than just proposing its own.



6.4.5 Alternative Approaches and Tool Choice
Not all plans will work on the first try:

Some approaches will fail due to limitations of the model or tools.
It’s valuable to try alternative methods and compare.

Tool choice matters:

GPT / ChatGPT – reasoning, summarising, planning, generating text.
Python / other tools – computation, heavy data processing, integration with external systems.

Often you manually choose when to ask the LLM to “do something” and when to switch to specialised tools.


6.4.6 Fixing and Spotting Errors

6.4.6.1 Fixing errors

Go back to the prompt before the error occurred and edit it.
Number steps in your plan so you can say: > “Repeat step 4, but show the intermediate table before filtering.”
Ask for explicit error reporting and logging.



6.4.6.2 Spotting hallucinations
Warning signs:

Input/output ratio is very small – tiny context, huge confident answer.
A lot of artificial data is generated without clear reason.
Long conversation history with many state changes.

Additional caution when:

Using conversation history as implicit input.
Re-running code cells on modified data without re-checking assumptions.




6.4.7 Consistency, Test Cases, and Source Linking
To build more trustworthy workflows:

Use identifiers and citations:

Page numbers, line numbers, section IDs.

Preserve references to original sources when summarising.
Build test cases:

Use synthetic data to test specific actions/conditions.
Check whether the workflow behaves as expected.




6.4.8 Breaking Down and Assembling Larger Projects

6.4.8.1 Breaking down a large project

Start by creating an index:

Sections, topics, questions.

Then use the index to drive operations:

“Using this index, extract all content related to X.”




6.4.8.2 Assembling output into a larger product
Incremental workflow:

Run analyses chunk by chunk.
Produce individual output files (markdown, figures, tables).
At the end, combine them into:

A report
A slide deck
A book chapter


This is particularly useful for text analysis:

First build an outline.
Then expand each section via incremental analysis.
Finally assemble using the outline as a backbone.




6.4.9 Turning Conversations into Software
You can move from interactive exploration to reusable tools. (From workflow to program)
Prompt example:

“Turn this process into a Python program that I can download and run locally. Include clear comments and command-line arguments.”

Good practice:

Inspect the code carefully before running it.
Prefer running in a safe environment (sandbox, container, virtualenv).
Keep configuration (file paths, parameters) outside the core logic where possible.

title: 6  Data analysis with ChatGTP
text:
6.5 Problem Selection and Trustworthy AI

6.5.1 Picking Good Problems for AI (ACHIEVE-aligned view)
Good AI candidates:

Easy to check whether the answer is correct.
A partial solution already saves substantial time.
The task benefits from alternative perspectives or reformulations.
The workflow can be decomposed into clear steps with observable outputs.

AI should augment, not replace, human judgment, creativity or intelligence.


6.5.2 The ACHIEVE Framework (Overview)
ACHIEVE is a way to think about how AI can augment human intelligence:

A – Aid human coordination
C – Cut tedium / Reduce tedious work
H – Provide a safety net (spot errors/risks)
I – Inspire creativity
E – Execute and scale ideas
V – Visibility and verification
E – Experimentation and exploration

Below, concrete examples and use cases.


6.5.3 ACHIEVE – Detailed Use Cases

6.5.3.1 Aid human coordination
Example: planning a workshop series.

Summarise meeting notes into key decisions and actions.
Identify actors and assign responsibilities.
Spot ambiguities and potential conflicts.
Propose clarifications and conflict-resolution options.
Draft follow-up emails and reminders.



6.5.3.2 Cut tedium / Reduce tedious work
Example: cleaning data from a registration form.

Map similar free-text entries onto consistent categories.
Create data dictionaries and lookup tables.
Group related terms and suggest standardised labels.
Generate code snippets for repetitive cleaning operations.
Visualise distributions to check for odd patterns.



6.5.3.3 Help provide a safety net
Example: travel reimbursement workflows.

Check forms for completeness and consistency.
Compare entries against internal rules or policies.
Highlight potential issues or missing information.
Suggest corrections or follow-up questions.
Important: final approval remains human.



6.5.3.4 Inspire creativity
Example: designing a workshop.

Ask it questions about your content to rethink structure:

“What natural modules do you see in this outline?”

Generate follow-up or bonus content ideas.
Suggest logistic setups and communication strategies.
Design templates for slides, handouts, and emails.
Help develop ideas into more detailed formats (e.g. exercises, case studies).



6.5.3.5 Execute and scale

Turn proven workflows into reusable templates.
Create “starter kits” (data + notebook + documentation).
Generate parameterised scripts for common tasks.
Build small internal tools that others can run with minimal effort.



6.5.3.6 Visibility and verification

Create diagrams of workflows and data flows.
Summarise long documents and highlight key decisions.
Create indexes and cross-reference tables.
Keep a clear link between outputs and their sources (citations, IDs).



6.5.3.7 Experimentation and exploration

Quickly test multiple approaches (alternative prompts, models, parameters).
Use synthetic data to explore edge cases safely.
Compare strategies side-by-side and reflect on trade-offs.




6.5.4 ACHIEVE for Augmented Intelligence (Recap)
The goal is to augment and amplify human creativity and problem-solving, not replace people.
ACHIEVE helps you:

Spend more time on high-value, human tasks.
Use AI as a thinking partner and productivity booster.
Support communication, alignment, and shared understanding.


6.5.4.1 Aid human communications

Draft email templates.
Summarise meetings and highlight open questions.
Clarify ambiguities and identify conflicts.
Map actors and actions across a project.



6.5.4.2 Cut tedious tasks

Automate repetitive formatting and cleaning.
Batch-generate routine outputs.
Scaffold code and documentation.



6.5.4.3 Help privide safety net
AI can:

Highlight ambiguities and potential conflict points.
Surface missing information or inconsistent logic.
Help evaluate risks and suggest mitigations.

But:

Humans remain responsible for final decisions.



6.5.4.4 Ideation

Generate many ideas quickly and cheaply.
Use AI for low-risk brainstorming and exploration.
Helpful for diagramming and visualising possibilities.
The human user:

Selects promising ideas.
Combines and adapts them.
Maintains ownership and direction of the process.




6.5.4.5 Extract and Filtering

Filter context information so reasoning stays tractable.
Summarise or analyse while keeping references to original sources.
Ensure filtering is immediately checkable (quote, cite, link).




6.5.5 Building Trustworthy AI
Dimensions of trustworthiness:

Veracity – conformity to facts.
Accuracy – numerical / logical correctness.
Cost of checking vs cost of producing the answer.

Remember:

Generative AI is not a primary source of facts.
Treat outputs as drafts to be checked, not final truth.

Good practices:

Mark outputs by certainty or evidence level.
Use visual aids (flow diagrams, decision trees) to help reasoning.
Apply risk assessments, especially for:

Physical risks
Social / psychological risks
Economic or career impacts
Data protection and privacy


AI can: - Point you to relevant sections in documents (tracing) - Maintain a “trail of generation” – where information came from. - Spot missing or fragmented documentation and help mitigate consequences.
This is especially useful with sensitive data, where you must know exactly:

What was used.
Why it was used.
How outputs were derived.

Remember the importance of expertise:

Appropriate domain expertise is crucial to interpret outputs.
AI cannot replace expertise; it can only amplify it.
In biomedical and clinical research, expert review is non-negotiable.

title: Notebook: Path to genAI
text:
A short history of generative AI – I started by simply using using tools ChatGPT [link] and Perplexity [link] to get some background: how we got here, which milestones really mattered, and who the main players and models are today.
ChatGPT, the basics – I subscribed to ChatGPT Pro (22 EUR/month) and worked through the beginner tutorials at the OpenAI Academy [link] (free). This was quick but surprisingly solid to build a foundation and understand what the tool can do (and what not) and how to use the interface.
Prompt engineering – To learn what I call “The art of talking to the machine”, I subscribed to Coursera [link] (42 EUR/month) and took some basic and advanced courses on prompt engineering by Jules White, including how to create custom AI assistants (Custom GPTs) and build trustworthy genAI. This is where I started to get some real insights
Data analysis with ChatGPT – Also by Jules White, these courses go deeper into practical workflows, showing how to use ChatGPT (via Code Interpreter) together with external tools for real data analysis tasks (and real magic).
Risks and Ethics of generative AI - A complication of insights and resources on how to provide appropriate rail guards for generative AI, AI agents and agentic AI and how (in my opinion) generative AI should be used ethically
